3748.prule: Struck 1918: 69 (Kresh-specific): no word stress. Stem and affix syllables are spoken with equal force, so that no main or secondary accent can be distinguished; the apparent accentuation of the stem syllable is an artefact of final-vowel reduction (and of whisper vowels before infixed *li), and words like kèléndi 'earring' only seem to carry a penultimate strong stress. p. 54 fn. 9 restates 'the absence of a strong stress (Starkton)'. Translation of the p. 69 passage: 'In general stem and affix syllables are pronounced with equal force, so that a main or secondary accent cannot be distinguished. An apparent accentuation of the stem syllable arises from the extensive reduction of final vowels, which moreover fluctuates in speech and occurs most often where final vowel and stem vowel have the same pitch, otherwise also with a low-toned final, most rarely with a high-toned final and a low-toned stem vowel. Since the whisper vowels arising before infixed *li are also pronounced with considerably less than normal force, some words, e.g. kèléndi "earring", easily give the false impression of a strong stress on the penultimate syllable, whereas an intensification of force does not in fact take place.'

3748.tone: All three sources describe Kresh as a tone language. Struck 1918: 67-69 ('1. Ton'): Hochton, Mittelton, Tiefton plus compound Hochtiefton and Tiefhochton; stem tones (Stammtöne), affix tones (Afformativtöne, dependent on stem tone, 'laws not yet clearly recognisable') and positional tones (Positionstöne) arising in word and sentence; fn. 9 p. 54 chooses the Christaller/Westermann tone notation 'bei dem Fehlen des Starktons und mit Rücksicht auf die Wiedergabe des Mitteltons'. Tucker & Bryan 1966 §2a: 'In the languages so far analysed for tone (BONGO, BAKA, MOROKODO, KRESH, YULU, KARA, SARA MBAI and to some extent BAGIRMI) three levels have been noted'; tone 'both lexical and grammatical'. Santandrea 1976 marks tone throughout; tone notation 'within Kresh... is limited to disyllables, which constitute the bulk of its vocabulary'; an excerpt speaks of 'two accented syllables' in gbó, kókó, gbómó, léle (tone marks). The stress question sits on top of this tone system: Struck denies word stress, T&B and Santandrea assert initial (plus suffixal) stress.

tn.translation: 1. Musical tone is of the greatest importance in Gbaya. By origin one must distinguish stem tones, affix (afformative) tones and positional tones; by pitch: low, mid, high and compound tones. … In the compound tones the second tone is regularly spoken as a mid tone before nasal clusters, so that I … could confine myself to marking high-low and low-high tones. … a) The stem tones are etymological throughout. … b) The affix tones depend on the tones of the stem syllables …

With a single final-vowel level/falling contrast a pitch-accent analysis is arguable, but every source frames Gimi as tonal; the verdict bin covers both.

3759.prule: Stress falls on the rightmost vowel of the ROOT in lexical words (nouns, verbs, adjectives); suffixes are invisible to stress (so a suffixed word such as /laːq-əl-tə-ˀj/ is [ˈlaːɢaldiˀj], stressed on the root, not the final syllable); compounds stress the rightmost root vowel of the rightmost member; preverbs (a closed adverbial class) are stressed on their leftmost vowel. 3760.tone: The 2008 sketch (inventory, syllable structure with a disyllabic-root constraint, vowel harmony, metaphony, final vowels, tones) never mentions stress, accent, prominence, feet or weight in its body; 'accent' appears only in bibliography titles (De Dominicis 2003 'Tone or Pitch Accent in Masa?'; 2004 'lingua ad accento tonale'). It describes two tonal registers H and L with lexical and aspectual contrasts of weak functional load and calls the tonal system endangered. Corroborating open sources by a second author: Guitang & Akumbu 2025 sec. 1.2 'In Gizey, words tend to be lexically specified with different tonal schemes. For example, nouns generally select between Low-Low, Low-High, High-Low, and Low-High-Low tonal schemes (Guitang 2024)'; Guitang 2025 (JALL) sec. 2.1 'Words in Gizey are generally monosyllabic or disyllabic' with lexical tone schemes; neither mentions word stress. De Dominicis 2006 (TAL) and 2010 (intonation) are tone-only; 'stress' in 2010 occurs only in a general passage on prominence, not as a Gizey rule. No source denies stress, so this is silence on stress within a tonal description, not a no word stress statement.

3762.prule: No stress rule is stated for Gobu. 'marque finale se rétracte sur une pénultième longue'; fn. 1 p. 418 'En gogo, tous les thèmes de forme -cvncv ont une voyelle longue' (so pre-nasal vowels count as long). Length itself is realised only on the penult/antepenult (Annexe 1.; p. 484). This conditions the placement of a H pitch accent, not of stress.
3764.dflt: antepenult (all short-vowel stems: 'tous les thèmes bi-moraïques ont une accentuation antépénultième'); realised as a falling tone on the penult when the word is disyllabic (fn. 3 p. 417).
3764.prule: Pitch-accent (H*) system, not stress: one culminative H per word, realised only on the penult or the antepenult, final syllable extrametrical. All short-vowel bimoraic stems take the H on the antepenult (íjego, múgulu, máfuta, íguva; on a disyllabic word it surfaces as a falling tone on the penult: mvûla, ndêje, mbêyu, ŋkûku). Stems with a long (penultimate) vowel take the H on the penult, on its first mora for reflexes of *BB/*HB/*HH (ŋóombe, cidóonda, ndóoto, ɲíimbo, ihéembe, síiŋgo) and on its second mora for reflexes of *BH (izoóya, ɲuúmba) — the residual lexical contrast ('4.: 2' schemes). Final H only in certain verb tenses and two loan nouns.

3764.tone: Philippson 1991 classifies Gogo as 'langue accentuelle à mélodie H*' (Annexe p. 509 item 3; key p. 497 item 3 = 'système tonal ou accentuel'), i.e. an accentual language whose accent is a single lexically placed H tone, with 2 prosodic schemes surviving in disyllabic nominal stems (item 4) and no Meeussen's rule (item 6 'absente'); 'langues à accent' p. 484; 'accent de mot strict' by analogy with Pokomo p. 496. He gives no intensity/stress statement, and Gogo is absent from his p. 483 lists of languages with a penultimate length or pitch culmination. Suleiman 2018 (UDOM MA, pp. 7-8) describes Gogo as having lexical H/L tone (kufú:ta 'to be impossible' vs kufû:ta 'wipe', credited to 'Rugemalira & Phanuel 2009') and relays Großerhode 1998 (Mpwapwa dialect): 'Gogo language is experiencing changes in its tonal system. The language is developing stress system to replace the tones and this process is going on with different speed and in different directions in different dialects.' No placement for that emerging stress is given anywhere opened. The two accounts converge on a restricted-tone / pitch-accent system in transition; the verdict codes Philippson's first-hand H-accent description.

3770.dq: Stress occurs on the base syllable of nouns and on the first syllable of verbs. [p. 32] ... Stress, which always occurs on the base, is not marked. [p. 55]
3770.dloc: Ch. 2 Phonology, p. 32, the paragraph directly under Table 2 'Table of Gurma Phonemes'; Ch. 3, p. 55, section 'The noun tonal patterns'.
3770.prule: Predictable, non-contrastive stress on the noun base (root): the first syllable of the base that follows the noun-class prefix (gi'badiga 'lizard', gi'janjaŋga 'bat' p. 27; mi'sagima 'itchiness', ti'pagidi 'praise' p. 28; li'papali 'carp' p. 26; o'yabinu 'size' p. 58) and on the first syllable of verbs, which carry no class prefix (o'pendi 'he has gone by' p. 18, o'bandi 'he has learned' p. 19, 'kali 'sit down' p. 27, 'boagidi 'to divide' p. 28). In effect root-initial stress; class prefixes and the subject pronoun o- are never stressed. Stress is left unmarked in the thesis's transcriptions because it is predictable; tone is the contrastive prosody.
3770.srule: Not described for present-day Gurma in Beckett 1974 (Ch. 2 Phonology, pp. 14, 32-42, 55 read: one predictable stress per word, on the noun base / verb-initial syllable; no secondary, rhythmic or alternating stress mentioned). The only occurrence of 'secondary stress' is App. 2, p. 148 fn. 1, where Beckett reads Koelle's (1854) accent mark on a noun-class prefix as a secondary stress beside primary stress on the base; no placement rule is given.
